The scale shapes here look like ones you already know, the minor and major pentatonic. They
sound different because their main notes sit in pitch areas. Charalampidis's warning: a minor
pentatonic played on the piano's keys over a major blues has "nothing blue about it". It is
like a French speaker trying to speak Chinese: the words are right and the accent gives them
away.

His names come from the degrees each scale has besides 1, 3 and 5. He also says the split into
separately named scales is for teaching. A blues player thinks of all the 3rds as one note.

**How to use the page.** Compare **▶ On the piano keys** with **▶ Shaded** in each scale. Start
the backing he uses for that scale: a major 12-bar, a power chord or a drone for the majorish
ones, the minor 12-bar for minorish, **One chord: I7♯9 / I7♭10** for neutral.

## Majorish 4-7

1, 3 (majorish), 4, 7, often with the 5. The 3rd is bent up from ♭3 into the upper part of its
area, close to the piano's 3. The 4th is a little high. The 7th is a little above ♭7. The 5th is
a little low and is reached by a bend from the 4th. A ♯4 just under the piano's can be added
too. Charalampidis suggests practising the four-note scale, the version with the 5th, and the
version with ♯4 and 5 separately, because each has its own colour.

<div class="bz" data-w="scale" data-set="panos" data-start="p47" data-title="The microtonal blues scales"></div>

### Eight ways to the majorish 3rd

On a fretted instrument, the bend is not the only way. Charalampidis shows these. He thinks the
slide and the hammer-on are why books treat ♭3 and 3 as two separate notes, when the move
between them is really one note.

<div class="bz" data-w="zone" data-deg="3" data-title="Ways to reach the 3rd"></div>

His list: a guitar slide (the bottleneck), with vibrato on a slightly raised ♭3; a slide from
fret to fret ♭3 → 3; a hammer-on ♭3 → 3; a trill; a fast bend and release, then a bend; a slide
to nowhere; and a bend behind the nut on an open string, which this page cannot play. He links
the bottleneck to one-string zithers in West and Central Africa and to the homemade *diddley
bow* (unverified here).

## Majorish 2-6

1 2 3 5 6, which looks like the major pentatonic. The 3rd is bent up from the 2nd. A lower
shade of the 3rd, just under ♭3, leads with the 2nd down to the key note or the 5th. The 2nd is
plain or a touch sharp. The 6th has a wider margin, from a little below the piano's 6 to a
little above it. Choose **“Majorish 2-6”** in the menu above.

## Extending and mixing

Each majorish scale can borrow the other's notes. 4-7 can take the 2nd and 6th, and 2-6 can
take the 4th and 7th, to make a seven-note scale. Charalampidis warns not to read these as
Dorian or Mixolydian, because those modes have no microtones. Mixing is different from
extending: you set up one scale's colour with a phrase, then switch to the other, often on a
chord change.

Choose a scale for each bar and press play. The site makes up a phrase in each bar from the
scale chosen (**New phrases** gives different ones). Try his example: 4-7 on the I chord, 2-6 on
the IV chord.

<div class="bz" data-w="chorus" data-form="major" data-plan="47,47,47,47,26,26,47,47,26,26,47,47" data-title="A 12-bar chorus: choose the scale bar by bar"></div>

The phrases are made by a simple random rule (stepwise moves through the scale, a longer note
at the end of every other bar). They show the colours. They are not Charalampidis's own licks.

## Minorish

Charalampidis thinks minor blues came later. Minor 12-bars became popular in the 1950s, and
British rock players wrote many more. The **minorish** scale is the 4-7 scale with only a small
bend on the 3rd, so it stays inside what is heard as minor. It can take a plain 2nd and 6th
(Dorian colour), or a ♭6, mostly over the iv chord (Aeolian colour). He hears B.B. King and
Albert King sometimes bend to the majorish 3rd over minor chords. He offers several possible
reasons: on purpose, habit, the blues habit of keeping melody and chords independent, or just
a slip.

<div class="bz" data-w="chorus" data-form="minor" data-plan="minorish,minorish,minorish,minorish,minorish,minorish,minorish,minorish,minorish,minorish,minorish,minorish" data-title="A minor 12-bar: minorish, or try neutral and majorish"></div>

## Neutral

The 4-7 scale with a **neutral 3rd**, halfway between the two. It fits songs on a tonic I7♯9,
the "Hendrix chord", which holds both 3rds. Charalampidis spells it **I7♭10** when it is the home
chord. More on that chord in [lesson 5](blues-tonality-harmony.qmd). Set the backing to **One
chord: I7♯9 / I7♭10** and choose **“Neutral”** above.
